messages.subject: Adding covariates
parts:
Hi Everyone,

I`m using transect data to estimate density in two habitat type.

I have three study sites and I have data from habitat 1 and habitat 2 in each site.

I`m using MCDS. I stratified by habitat and added site, and season (winter, migration) as covariates. I added them as fields under my line transects layer.

I`m using Transect ID (label) and transect length (Decimal) as field in the Line transect layer as well.

The only options I have for `kind of field` when I add site and season are: Integer, text and decimal. I picked text.

When I run the models Distance recognizes only on level for site (it should have two levels, habitat 1 and habitat2) and one level for season...

I must be missing something when I`m adding the new field to the data base.

Help/advice will be appreciated :)

Thanks

Ana

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Adding covariates
parts:
Ana, I’m assuming you ticked the box to indicate that these were factor-type covariates.  Not sure what you mean when you say that Distance only recognises one level.  You should only get one parameter estimate for each of habitat and season.  When you have 2 levels of a factor, you have just one parameter to estimate the difference between them.  So Distance essentially fits a detection function assuming one level, then gives you a parameter estimate telling you how the scale parameter of the detection function changes for the other level.  But you should get a plot of the estimated detection function for each habitat type and for each season.

 

Steve Buckland

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Re: Adding covariates
parts:
Not sure what you mean by 'asked results by sample'.  Estimation tends to be poor when you do this, as sample sizes tend to be small.  If you do do it, you need to assume a common model for the detection function.  You could not fit a different detection function model for each sample.  There will be confounding - e.g. only one habitat recorded at some samples.

Steve
